tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — FEW NARROW RACEMES
tiles.details: Thin paspalum is a tufted or short-rhizomatous perennial, often 25–110 cm across treatments. Terminal and sometimes axillary racemes may be partly hidden in the leaf sheaths. Panels 1 and 3 show genuine flowering portions but not a rooted whole Texas plant. Do not assign a variety from a flowering branch alone. NEW gallery panel 5 (index4) now shows actual source-identified field-growing thin paspalum with basal green leaves and elongated fertile stems in their habitat, not just a cut seedhead. Its flowering stalks are among overlapping plants so one crown-to-head path is still somewhat obstructed; source observation belongs to botanist Alex Abair, Florida not Hays.
tiles.short: Usually one or two slender one-sided racemes, occasionally several; examine a whole flowering culm.
tiles.status: REAL FIELD-GROWING LEAFY TUFT PHOTO NOW COVERED — HAYS VOUCHER STILL OPEN

tiles.heading: 02 · INNER TRUE LIGULE AND HAIR PLACEMENT
tiles.details: Open the blade–sheath junction at 10–20× and measure the free membrane with a 1-mm reference. Leaf blade margins and sheaths may be variably hairy, including papillose-based hairs in some varieties; the source blade photograph cannot prove individual hair bases or the true membrane. Do not use hairiness alone to name a variety.
tiles.short: Very short membranous ligule about 0.2–0.5 mm; separate adjacent white hairs.
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — CALIBRATED TRUE LIGULE AND MARGIN HAIRS

tiles.heading: 03 · PAIRED MATURE SPIKELETS
tiles.details: Inspect attached ripe spikelets at 10–20× with a millimeter scale. Each spikelet encloses one lower sterile and one upper fertile floret; two adjacent spikelets are not two florets. Purple protruding organs in panel 1 are anthers and stigmas, NOT purple seeds or awns. Current pictures do not establish calibrated spikelet length.
tiles.short: Small, flattened spikelets about 1.4–2.6 mm, often in pairs along one side.
tiles.status: REAL FLOWERING SPIKELETS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO MEASURED MATURE PAIRS

tiles.heading: 04 · ABSENT LOWER GLUME; TWO DISTINCT LEMMAS
tiles.details: At 20–40× dissect one mature spikelet. The upper glume is approximately spikelet-length and usually three-veined; the lower sterile lemma is also thin and about spikelet-length. The upper fertile lemma is hardened with incurved margins and an enclosed palea. No long projecting lemma awn is expected. Fine hairs and glume veins must not be arrowed unless pixels resolve them.
tiles.short: Lower glume absent or obscure; upper glume and sterile lemma thin; fertile lemma hard and awnless.

tiles.heading: 05 · DISTICHUM AND PUBIFLORUM LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Paspalum distichum commonly has two terminal racemes, spikelets about 2.4–4 mm and true rooted aboveground stolons in wet ground. P. pubiflorum often has several racemes and about 2.7–3.2 mm spikelets. Branch counts and size can overlap; verify actual rooted habit, mature spikelets and glume pubescence. Panel 2 is PUBIFLORUM, explicitly a different species. Avoid variety-level claims without same-plant foliage anatomy. NEW original large Dallisgrass CC BY-SA4 photographed 5mm spikelet plate (gallery panel6, index5) is explicitly another INTRODUCED species, while the existing P. pubiflorum (panel2,index1) is another differently identified grass. Compare little pale thin paspalum spikelets against larger silk-margined Dallisgrass, but glumes have NOT been dissected in P. setaceum.
tiles.short: Thin paspalum: few racemes, small spikelets; knotgrass: rooted stolons; pubiflorum: often larger spikelets.
tiles.status: ACTUAL TWO-TAXON COMPARISON PHOTO PAIR COVERED — MATCHED SIZE/GLUME DISSECTION MISSING

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE / TWO HANDOFFS
tiles.details: Current actual photos in GitHub: FOUR physically archived target-species CC BY4 Alex Abair JPEGs including NEW naturally growing tuft and full culm image 49099738, macro of real paired pale spikelets with purple floral organs, source full raceme photo, and blade margin photo. Two different-species look-alike gallery panels: hairyseed paspalum iNat CC BY-NC conditional site-use verification and introduced Dallisgrass CC BY-SA4 author-scaled macro (locally hosted in Dallisgrass canonical folder). Score is based on actual visible anatomy; no source-authenticated tiny 0.2–0.5mm inner ligule, root crown, measured isolated glumes/lemma or same-scale Hays vouchered comparative image. No variety-level native range/taxonomy inference. Public Pages and mobile arrow QA not verified.
tiles.short: Four licensed local exact thin-paspalum JPEGs; true inner 0.2–0.5-mm membrane still missing.
tiles.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — TARGETS: INNER LIGULE, DISSECTED SPIKELETS, ROOT CONNECTION

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: THIN PASPALUM (P. setaceum complex): small/medium Paspalum with one to a few narrow one-sided racemes; different varieties may vary in foliage hairiness. The original close-up shows oval green spikelets with PURPLE exserted floral parts, and a second credited Alex Abair view now shows the full slim flowering branch beside a leaf. Don't identify variety by one flower photo.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Use the paired flower macro and full raceme photo to teach head/flower organization; photograph same-plant foliage, ligule, maturity and glume traits with ruler before any variety ID.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Open the blade–sheath junction at 10–20× and measure the free membrane with a 1-mm reference. Leaf blade margins and sheaths may be variably hairy, including papillose-based hairs in some varieties; the source blade photograph cannot prove individual hair bases or the true membrane. Do not use hairiness alone to name a variety.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Thin paspalum is a tufted or short-rhizomatous perennial, often 25–110 cm across treatments. Terminal and sometimes axillary racemes may be partly hidden in the leaf sheaths. Panels 1 and 3 show genuine flowering portions but not a rooted whole Texas plant. Do not assign a variety from a flowering branch alone. NEW gallery panel 5 (index4) now shows actual source-identified field-growing thin paspalum with basal green leaves and elongated fertile stems in their habitat, not just a cut seedhead. Its flowering stalks are among overlapping plants so one crown-to-head path is still somewhat obstructed; source observation belongs to botanist Alex Abair, Florida not Hays.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Narrow racemes are not enough: compare wet-ground creeping P. distichum (often 2 branch V and TRUE rooted stolons) and P. pubiflorum (often several racemes and more robust 2.7–3.2 mm oval spikelets). Purple parts are anthers/stigmas, NOT purple grains. Record blade and sheath surface hairs by actual macro.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

intro: THIN PASPALUM (P. setaceum complex): small/medium Paspalum with one to a few narrow one-sided racemes; different varieties may vary in foliage hairiness. The original close-up shows oval green spikelets with PURPLE exserted floral parts, and a second credited Alex Abair view now shows the full slim flowering branch beside a leaf. Don't identify variety by one flower photo.
memory_rule: COUNT COMPLETE RACEMES → MEASURE 5 RIPE SPIKELETS → CHECK MARGINAL HAIRS → ROOTED BASE/COLLAR. DALLIS few large silky; VASEY many small silky; FLORIDA few big round; PUBIFLORUM smaller oval; SETACEUM narrow variable; DISTICHUM two + real stolons.
safety_note: Gross photo structures are references, NOT expert confirmation. Even new licensed images are PROVISIONAL — USER PHOTO REVIEW PENDING and not proof of Hays County presence.
field_rule: P. setaceum often has one to few narrow racemes with relatively small spikelets and highly variable varieties differing in blade hairiness. Creeping wet-ground P. distichum typically has two terminal racemes and obvious stolons, while P. pubiflorum often has several racemes and larger spikelets. A single closeup of spikelets is not enough to prove variety.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Narrow racemes are not enough: compare wet-ground creeping P. distichum (often 2 branch V and TRUE rooted stolons) and P. pubiflorum (often several racemes and more robust 2.7–3.2 mm oval spikelets). Purple parts are anthers/stigmas, NOT purple grains. Record blade and sheath surface hairs by actual macro.
